$comment: This repository's claims ladder, declared as data. It is `proofs/README.md`'s own ladder — what is PROVED, what is only TESTED, what is ASSUMED — in a schema a tool can read, so the question does not have to be answered by reading prose and hoping two documents use the same words. A `not claimed` item is the ABSENCE of a row, never a row: the README enumerates those, and enumerating them here would turn a disclaimer into a claim. Levels are the closed set proved | tested | assumed | policy. Authored by hand, never generated — editing the ladder means editing this file and the README together. Since Phase 144 it is CHECKED rather than trusted: the proof leg's host step runs the `Proofs.Ladder` family (tests/Fuaran.Core.Tests/ProofsLadderTests.fs), which holds every row to the tree — a proved row's theorem is a top-level declaration of the model it names, that model is one `proofs/check.ps1` actually checks, a tested row's named cases exist in the `Proofs.Oracle` family, every checked module has a proved row, and the phase citations and levels are the closed forms. Since Phase 174 an `assumed` row also carries a `class`, from the closed set domain-obligation | model-bridge | premise, saying WHICH KIND of assumed it is: a `domain-obligation` is what a domain owes when it instantiates this substrate and carries `dischargedBy`, the `Conformance` law whose green run at that domain's own witness is the sampled discharge; a `model-bridge` is what this repository's own model has not bridged and carries `closes` — a `fuaran-core#NNN` phase, `permanent` where nothing could close it, or `unscheduled` where something could and nobody has taken it; a `premise` is what is permanently assumed and what no run of anything discharges. The same family holds every class, every law name (against the shipped kit's declared law-family roster, `Fuaran.Core.Families`, whose own completeness is held to reflection over the shipped assembly BY RETURN TYPE — Phase 184 narrowed this from the `Conformance` module's whole public static surface, so an obligation can no longer name a law that no conformance census enumerates) and every `closes` form to the tree. Row-to-tree agreement only, with ONE prose exception: the `Core-to-domain proof contract` table in `proofs/README.md` is PARSED and held to this file row for row, because a contract a domain reads and a ladder a tool reads that disagree are worse than either alone. Whether a row says the same thing as the README's surrounding prose is still a human act.

claims.claim: On the model, for every N and every permutation of a lane set, the fold halts with the same canonical conflict report or folds to the same state. Proved with no assume and no admit under --report_assumes error; the fold half under `independence_diamond` for a lane set whose lanes all apply from the base, the halt half under no hypothesis at all.
Every decode combinator reaches exactly one outcome on every input, and which one is characterised structurally — so the failure classification is exhaustive rather than merely non-empty.

The recursive node decoder is total on an arbitrary JSON value and succeeds on exactly the well-formed documents. Termination is content here rather than a formality: the decoder descends into a child array obtained by name, so nothing structural is visible at the call site.
Decoding an encoded node returns that node, for every node of the reference vocabulary, at every depth.

On every document the read policy does not name, the tolerant and strict readers accept the same values and refuse the same documents — a promise about the VERDICT, not about the message; on a document with no null at all the two are literally the same function.

WIRE_FORMAT §2 rule 2's obligation on the decoder, as a theorem: on two documents that differ only by the ORDER of object members, at any depth, every decode combinator answers the same. The scalar readers, kindOf, strField, intField and mapList return EQUAL outcomes, message included; getProp, whose result is itself a reordered subtree, returns a related one. Duplicate-free member lists only — see duplicate-keys-break-order-invariance for why that premise cannot be dropped.

WIRE_FORMAT §20's one-answer rule at this layer: the kind-dispatch node decoder returns the SAME TREE on a document whose object members have been reordered at any depth — literally equal, since a decoded node carries no members of its own — or the same named refusal.

The converse direction, which is what keeps the invariance above from being vacuous: the relation CONTAINS every reordering of a duplicate-free member list whose values are themselves related — one level of a deep reordering, with the scalar arms as the base cases. A relation nothing is related by would satisfy every invariance lemma and say nothing.

The premise is NECESSARY, not convenient: two documents that are the same members in a different order, whose keys repeat, and getProp answers differently. Nothing upstream excludes them — the parser appends every member with no key check, and Phase 146's model says so — so the duplicate-free premise is carried by this theorem rather than inherited, and a session weakening the relation to a plain list permutation reddens this lemma first.

NO `JVal` CONTAINS A NULL, at any depth — WIRE_FORMAT section 2 rule 4's value half, which was prose and a comment on the type until this phase. Stated over the one model here that HAS a null, the foreign document of the read-policy section, so it is a statement and not a tautology: every wire value, viewed as a document, is null-free and reads back as EXACTLY itself under either read policy; the strict reader accepts EXACTLY the null-free documents, an iff; and whatever EITHER reader returns is null-free — the tolerant policy erases an object-member null, it never carries one through. Proved under no hypothesis at all. The encoder's half is `no-null-rendered`. NOT claimed: anything about a host, which may hold nulls of its own in its own types; this is about what a document can contain once it is a `JVal`.

NO VALUE A DECODE COMBINATOR RETURNS CAN CARRY A FUNCTION, at any depth — the type half of 'a closure crosses the wire only as the string "<closure>"' (section 2 rule 10, section 4). The lemma is that every type a combinator or the node decoder returns, and the wire value and the foreign document model themselves, has DECIDABLE EQUALITY: F* derives `hasEq` for an inductive only when every constructor argument has it and derives it for no arrow type, so this is the prover's own certificate that the closed value type has no function-typed component. The closure sentinel is a string like any other. The control was run both ways before the lemma was believed: a type with one function-typed constructor argument cannot be declared without `noeq`, and declared with it the same lemma fails to prove. NOT claimed: anything about a HOST, a `Custom` renderer or a host-call seam — a registered function is host code the wire merely NAMES, which the UI language estate's escape-hatch inventory enumerates and these lemmas do not — nor about a decoder handed to the array walker, which is the domain's own function and not a wire value.

NO COMBINATOR INSPECTS A STRING VALUE, so the closure sentinel is inert. Replacing one string by another throughout a document COMMUTES with every combinator — under no premise, and word for word: every refusal is the same refusal, message included (`sentinel_inert_combinators`) — and with the node decoder: the same documents decode, the same documents are refused, and the decoded node is the original with the same replacement made. The sentinel is the instance (`closure_sentinel_is_a_string`), not a special case; member KEYS are untouched, since a key is a name the decoder asks for and not a value it is handed. The phase asked for decoding to be INVARIANT under replacing the sentinel with ANY string, and that wording was wrong twice: it is EQUIVARIANT, which is the stronger and the true statement, and 'any' fails in one position — see `sentinel-tag-position-is-the-exception`. The node-level premise is exactly that neither string is one of the vocabulary's own kind tags, which the sentinel satisfies.

The premise of `sentinel-inert` is NECESSARY, and it is the vocabulary's own dispatch rather than any combinator that makes it so: a document whose `kind` member IS the sentinel is refused as an unknown kind, and rewriting the sentinel into a kind tag makes it decode — so 'replace it with any other string' is false in exactly the tag position, and the two outcomes are proved NOT related. That is a domain reading its own discriminator, not a payload being inspected, and a future session weakening the premise goes red here first.

Every corpus fixture and every generated document, with the members of every object reordered at every depth, seeded and replayable: production's answers on the shuffle are compared against its own answers on the original — equality for every combinator whose result carries no members, the extracted outcome_perm for getProp, whose result is itself reordered — and the oracle is compared against production on the shuffled document. This is the case the corpus structurally cannot present, every fixture in it being canonically ordered. Each pair is checked to be an instance of the extracted member_perm, duplicate-keyed documents are filtered by the extracted keys_unique_deep, and a getProp that reads the FIRST member rather than the named one is required to lose.

claims.claim: That the order production picks and the order the model computes are the same order, on the base-plus-N-chains shape. Two lemmas: a distinct enumeration of a spine's closure in which every node follows its single parent is that spine in append order (`spine_order_forced`, a list argument naming no DAG and no hash), and the frontier drain over that closure produces such an enumeration (`kahn_drain_is_such_an_enumeration`). The recovery is therefore restated with the order universally quantified rather than fixed to the parent-walk reversal (`between_chain_any_order`), and the fold above it with it (`reconcile_many_dag_ordered_eq`, `fold_once_dag_ordered_eq`). The smallest-id tie-break is NOT modelled and does not need to be: the selector is a parameter constrained only to return a member of the frontier it is handed, and on a spine that frontier is one element wide at every step (`kahn_frontier_singleton`), so every selector agrees and nothing here says how ids compare. The order over a MERGE DAG, where the frontier genuinely widens and the tie-break becomes observable, was left unclaimed here and is PROVED since Phase 156, at `general-topological-order`; this row's spine results are corollaries of that one, re-derived at its selector (`spine_drain_is_the_parent_walk`, `spine_drain_is_append_order`).

The id-ordered Kahn drain over an ABSTRACT node set — no base, no lanes, no hash — is DETERMINISTIC, a function of the node set alone and invariant under the order the nodes arrived (`drain_deterministic`, stated over the module's own permutation relation); a LINEAR EXTENSION of the parent relation over every node it places (`drain_linear_extension`); and TOTAL on an acyclic set, placing every node exactly once and producing a topological enumeration (`drain_total_on_acyclic`). Acyclicity is taken as a topological enumeration supplied as a witness list, which is the standard characterisation and is not circular — the witness is never the drain's own output — and `drain_complete_is_acyclic` gives the converse from the linear-extension theorem, so complete drain and acyclic set are an IFF, which is exactly the length comparison `Dag.isAcyclic` / `Dag.tryTopoOrder` make. This is where the smallest-id tie-break stops being decoration: `frontier` answers in the work list's order, so only an order-invariant selector survives `drain_deterministic`, and Phase 142's `pick_head` does not. The id order is a PARAMETER constrained to be a total order, so the claim is that clones sharing an order agree rather than that any particular order is production's — the differential ties it to `String.CompareOrdinal`, which is what `List.sort` gives a string list. Phase 142's spine results are corollaries at this selector. NOT claimed: the delta RECOVERY over a merge DAG, which stays at `dag-delta-recovery`'s shape; `Dag.mergeBase`; and any consumer's own instantiation.

What the drain does with a parent OUTSIDE the set is a parameter of the model, because the two production call sites differ on it and a theorem about "the drain" that did not say which would be a theorem about neither. `IgnoreDangling` is `Dag.topoCore`'s closure walk with `Dag.ancestorsOf`'s `ContainsKey` guard and the `parentsIn` filter that follows — the parent never enters the closure, is filtered out of the in-degree, constrains nothing, and the drain proceeds; it is the policy on the fold path (`topoOrder` to `between` to `betweenOps` to `reconcileMany` to `foldOnce`) and on `replayTo`. `RefuseDangling` is `Dag.firstBreak`'s `MissingParent`, hence `verifyDag` and `fromJsonlVerified`, which refuse the whole set before any drain runs. `drain_policies_agree` proves the two are the same function on a set holding every parent it names, so the fold path pays nothing for the refusing one's existence; `drain_refusal_characterised` proves the refusal fires exactly when a parent lies outside, and `drain_refusal_needs_a_dangler` the converse. The refusal names the SMALLEST offending id rather than the first in the work list, matching `firstBreak`'s `Map.toList` id-ordered scan, which is what lets `drain_deterministic` cover the refusing policy too. NOT modelled: the refusal's diagnostic payload — `firstBreak` reports the missing parent beside the node, and the node determines it.

The extracted drain, instantiated at `String.CompareOrdinal`, run beside `Dag.tryTopoOrder` over the same nodes — per LANE HEAD, whose closure is a spine and where no tie-break can be wrong, and per MULTI-HEAD UNION built with `Dag.merge`, where the frontier is N wide once the base is drained and the tie-break decides the sequence. The adequacy guard is the frontier WIDTH: a run whose frontier never passed one node re-measured the spine under another name, and the case fails by number rather than passing quietly. The go-red is a model draining LARGEST-id-first — as legitimate a selector as the model's own, since it still returns a member of the frontier it is handed — run over the unions and not the lane heads, because a one-element frontier has one minimum and one maximum. Three cases ride with it: every permutation of the node set drained and compared against the set's own drain; the two policies, agreeing on a parent-closed closure and diverging the moment the base node is dropped from it; and a hand-built cyclic set, unreachable through `Dag.append`, where production's `isAcyclic` must see the cycle and the model's drain must stop at the same short prefix, with an acyclic control beside it. Agreement is over the sets drawn, never over all inputs.

claims.claim: For the skeleton-op tree algebra, two operations whose footprints are declared disjoint and which both apply at an id-unique tree each apply after the other and reach the same tree — the fold theorem's domain hypothesis, proved rather than sampled, for ALL FIFTEEN unordered operation pairs since Phase 162 lifted the diamond along a batch's script; it covered twelve of the fifteen when Phase 133 shipped it, and the three it left are `tree-algebra-batch-nesting`, which is now a proved row rather than an assumed one. Nine of the fifteen are closed by the conservative footprint alone and never look at a tree: a remove or a move writes an unknown parent, independence refuses that against any structural write, and every skeleton operation except a do-nothing batch writes structure — so such a pair is independent only where the other operation does nothing at all.

The unknown-parent over-approximation in `Ops.independent` is NECESSARY over the `Footprint` record as it stands, not merely conservative: no predicate over the four address sets can widen the promise. Proved at one well-formed tree by three facts — a relocation that MOVES a node and a structural write under a parent inside the moved subtree do commute, with every clause but the pinned relocation pair already satisfied (`relocation_disjoint_diamond`); the same shape with a REMOVE in it does not, because the structural write's parent is destroyed with the subtree (`relocation_diamond_fails_for_a_remove`); and the two operations carry byte-identical footprints (`relocation_footprints_coincide`). One verdict therefore covers both, so freeing the safe pair frees the fatal one. A single witness refutes the universal claim. This is also the second pinned over-approximation — a remove's content-write records the target id and not its tree-unknown subtree — shown to be load-bearing for the first, which STABILITY.md had asserted in prose since Phase 78. NOT claimed: anything about what a WIDER record would admit, or the general move-versus-structural-write theorem, which is true and deliberately unproved because no clause could consume it.

The pairs the pinned clause refuses, enumerated: exactly {a relocating operation} x {an operation that is not inert}, both ways round — `still_refused`, the contrapositive of `relocating_forces_inert`. Part of that set is GENUINELY dependent and could not be freed by any footprint record whatever: two `MoveNode`s whose destinations sit inside each other's subtrees each apply alone and reject each other with `WouldNestUnderSelf`, because the obstruction is the cycle check rather than the addresses (`relocation_move_pair_also_fails`). So the refused set is not one homogeneous class waiting on a better footprint. No claim is made here about the remove-versus-remove, remove-versus-move or remove-versus-reorder members, which Phase 143 did not examine.

The precision-ceiling witness run on the EXTRACTED model and on production `Ops.footprint` / `Ops.independent` / `Ops.apply` side by side, over the reference domain: the same two operations are footprint-indistinguishable in both, both refuse the pair, the move commutes in both and the remove-shaped batch diverges in both. A decision not to change something survives only as a check that goes red when someone does, and this is that check. Agreement is over this witness, never over all inputs.

claims.claim: Fold confluence for the skeleton-op tree algebra with NO domain hypothesis remaining, over the WHOLE skeleton operation alphabet since Phase 162 — batch included and nested to any depth, where Phase 133 shipped it over the four non-batch operations: the same lanes reach the same tree however they arrive, a lane set that cannot fold halts with the same canonical report however it arrives, and none folds under one order and halts under another. The halt half is proved separately under no hypothesis at all — not the diamond, not id uniqueness, nothing about the apply engine.

Phase 137 fixed the validator and Phase 138 lifted the model to it, so this is no longer a claim about the LIVE algebra — the counterexample and the clause it is about are named `insert_breaks_wf_pre137` and `apply_pre137`, and the refutation stands exactly as it did. What it refuted is now TRUE and proved, at `apply-preserves-wf`; that the fix closes THIS counterexample is proved at `insert-subtree-check-closes-it`. Proved beside it throughout, and unchanged: the conditional form `ins_wf` and its converse `ins_wf_conv`, which were the specification the fix had to meet.

The extracted tree model agrees with the shipped apply engine and footprint derivation over the generated operation pool and every state a prefix of it reaches — the footprint as four address sets, the verdict, an accepted result through the content hash computed by production's own function on both sides, and a rejection by class. Every rejection class the plain apply can raise is asserted reached BY NAME rather than counted, and a bridge that erases every kind tag is required to make the result comparison fail, so a green report is known to be one that can lose.

claims.claim: The tree the algebra runs over carries each id at most once. This is a hypothesis rather than an oversight: the lookup that resolves an id returns the FIRST match in document order, so on a tree carrying one id twice what it returns is a fact about the order as well as the contents — and a reorder moves the order, which makes the diamond FALSE there rather than merely unproved. Nothing in the estate produces such a tree and the structural diff refuses one outright, but no shipped type carries the invariant. NARROWED BY PHASE 138 to what it now is — a hypothesis about the INPUT alone. Until Phase 137 the algebra could also break the invariant on a tree that had it (`insert-breaks-id-uniqueness`); since Phase 138 that half is a theorem, `apply-preserves-wf`, so a tree that starts id-unique stays id-unique under every accepted operation. What remains unenforced is the entry point, and only the entry point.

evidence.assumption: the tree the fold runs over carries each id at most once

claims.claim: CLOSED BY PHASE 162, and the row is rewritten in place rather than retired because what it assumed and how it stopped being an assumption is the useful part of it. It carried, from Phase 133: the proved diamond covers twelve of the fifteen operation pairs, and the three left open are one shape — either side a batch that neither does nothing nor relocates. Lifting the leaf diamond along a batch script is the argument the fold theorem already performs at lane granularity, and it needs the id-uniqueness invariant at each intermediate state of the script. Phase 138 supplied that invariant and did not perform the lift, so the boundary moved from waiting on a theorem to waiting on labour — a distinction this row was rewritten once already to record. Phase 162 did the induction: independence descends through a union, the leaf diamond lifts along a script by induction threading the invariant at each step, and the guarded algebra's diamond follows, so `covered` is deleted and the alphabet is the whole of the skeleton operations. One correction that matters for anyone reading the history: the lift did NOT consume `apply-preserves-wf`, which every earlier note names — the residue is exactly the pairs where neither side relocates, so the operations involved are inserts, reorders and nests of them, for which the per-operation preservation lemmas were already in the model. `Preservation.fst` opens `TreeOps.fst` and could not have been cited from it in any case.

On an id-unique tree, a node's parent PRECEDES it in the preorder walk — the fact Phase 141 named when it deferred the diff's reconstruction, proved over the model's own preorder. Two things about its shape are worth reading before citing it. It is a theorem of the WALK rather than an invariant an edit could break: the walk emits a node before its subtree by construction, and id uniqueness is needed only so that the parent's occurrence is the first one, which is what makes `precedes` well defined at all. So preservation by insert, remove and reorder is the COROLLARY that each preserves id uniqueness, and the remove's form is over the SURVIVORS — a removed subtree's positions do not move, they vanish, and a statement over the original tree's nodes would be false on exactly the nodes the operation exists to destroy. The ordering predicate is written without indices, the same decision the model makes about `List.sort` and `List.length`, and its direction is pinned by evaluation because an ordering predicate written backwards makes every theorem over it true and none of them meaningful.

The preorder-position lemma under ANY accepted operation, batch included: if a well-formed tree accepts an operation, then in the tree it hands back a node's parent still precedes it in the walk. It is `apply-preserves-wf` composed with `preorder-parent-first`, and it lives beside the first of those because the remove clause's well-formedness lemma is that module's and the tree model cannot cite it — that module opens this one. `rem_preserves_parent_first` states the remove alone, in the survivor form. This is the statement a reconstruction argument cites; what it does NOT give is the same fact about the tree in hand at step k of a script, which is a different quantifier and is the induction the diff's reconstruction still needs.

A content-addressed DAG grown from nothing by append and merge alone, each naming parents the DAG already held, has no integrity break; and a linear hash chain grown from genesis by append alone verifies. The id half is free by construction, but the parent half is not: append does not check that the parent it is handed names a node the DAG holds, so every-parent-present is a precondition on how a DAG was grown rather than a property of the constructor, and the theorem carries it as one. Its PREMISE is the whole of nothing: `intact_verifies` takes no injectivity hypothesis of any kind — not the hash's, not the codec's, not the splices' — because append mints the id from the content it is storing, so the id cannot be wrong however weak the hash is. Phase 145 left it untouched for that reason; there was nothing there to decompose.

claims.claim: `Canon.render` reaches a rendering on every value — carried by its type, since F* admits a definition only after showing it defined everywhere and terminating — and WHICH constructor produced a rendering is determined by its FIRST CHARACTER: a string opens with a quote, an array with a bracket, an object with a brace, a boolean with one of two letters, a number with a numeric character, and never with a closing or separating one. That is what makes the encoder's shape dispatch exhaustive rather than merely non-empty, the same distinction `decode-total` draws on the decode side, and it is the fact the reader's own dispatch turns on at every position.

A reader for exactly the grammar `Canon.render` emits is a LEFT INVERSE of it on the canonical subset, in every trailing context: reading the rendering of a value followed by anything returns that value's normal form and the anything, unchanged. This is the engine of the phase — every other proved row here is a corollary of it — and it is what makes the canonical form's converse a construction rather than an induction over byte lists. It is deliberately NOT a second model of `Json.parse`: that parser has theorem 4, and what injectivity needs is the existence of an inverse rather than a second account of production's own.

EQUAL BYTES IMPLY EQUAL VALUES, up to the object-member order rule 2 normalises away: two canonical values that render identically have the same normal form. This is the converse WIRE_FORMAT section 2 never stated and that every digest in the estate silently rests on — the op-stream chain id, the DAG content id, the teleport digest and cross-host attestation all hash this rendering and read hash equality as value equality, and `op-codec-injective-certified` leaves a codec's own injectivity to the codec precisely because one built on `Canon.render` inherits it only if `Canon.render` has it. `render_injective_on_normal` is the literal form on values whose members are already in key order, which is the shape every value a reader returns has.

EQUAL VALUES IMPLY EQUAL BYTES — section 2's own promise that the twelve rules make the encoding deterministic, proved rather than asserted, for values equal up to the member order rule 2 normalises away. With `canonical-form-injective` it is an iff (`canonical_form_iff`), which is what the words 'canonical form' mean and is more than either half. The sorting half of it is where rule 2 is doing the work: under the comparator's total-order premises the sort is idempotent and depends only on the members, so the author's key order carries no information into the bytes at all.

The REFUTATION, and the reason the two rows above are stated over a subset and up to member order rather than flatly. `render a == render b ==> a == b` is FALSE of the shipped encoder four ways, each proved for EVERY instantiation rather than exhibited at a contrived one: a non-finite float renders as the quoted string of its token and therefore as that STRING (`render_aliases_nan` and its two siblings); a finite float whose layout carries no point and no exponent renders as the INTEGER of that token, which is the numeric normalisation `JVal`'s own type doc names; the two zeroes are one token, by rule 5's collapse; and two objects differing only in authored member order are one byte sequence, by rule 2's sort. The fourth is not a loss but the purpose of a canonical form. The first is the finding: unlike `Json.render`, which has the guarded `Json.tryRender` beside it, `Canon` has no guarded counterpart, so a digest over a non-finite float collides with the digest over the string a reader decodes it back to and nothing refuses it. (That last sentence was the state at Phase 149 and is still true of `Canon.render`, whose bytes did not move. Phase 165 added the guarded counterpart beside it: see `canonical-render-guard`.)

`Canon.render` NEVER EMITS THE TOKEN `null` — not at the root, not at any depth, for ANY value, including those outside the canonical subset the rows above are stated over. Section 2 rule 4's encoder half. The statement is LEXICAL on purpose: 'the rendering does not contain n-u-l-l' is false, since the string "null" renders those four characters inside a literal, so the model carries the three-state lexer every JSON reader has and proves something stronger than the absence of one token — outside a string literal the renderer emits ONLY structural punctuation, the characters of a numeral and the letters of `true` and `false`. There is no bare `n` anywhere in a rendering, hence no `null` at any position that lies outside a literal, and the grammar's own reader has no arm that accepts one (`reader_refuses_null`). Rule 6 is what carries the argument: an escaped body never closes its own literal. ONE premise, `layouts_numeric` — both of rule 5's layouts are numerals — weaker than `tok_read_ok` and recorded on `canon-numeral-layouts`. NOT claimed: `Canon.renderOrdered`, which is not modelled; JSON a host writes by any other route; or that the byte sequence never appears, which it correctly does inside strings.

What did NOT move: the contract's other two clauses, which are `propagation-change-set-and-prior` below.

Production detects an undeclared read by INSTRUMENTING the resolver it hands `evalNode`: the resolver records the ids it is asked for, and the walk refuses on the first one outside the declaration. claims.claim: `QueryRegistry.dispatch` of an id the registry does not hold is the typed refusal `NoSuchQuery id known`, naming the id and every id the registry does hold — and the result is the SAME under every host resolver, which is what "runs no resolver" means for a pure function without instrumenting one. `invoke` can never produce the registry's two refusals (`invoke_never_registry_refusal`), so the classes stay disjoint: a `NoSuchQuery` is always the registry's answer and never a resolver's. The resolver is the model's parameter and stays outside the claim: nothing here is a theorem about any resolver.

An argument set `validateParams` rejects makes `invoke` return that rejection, for every resolver alike — no resolver ran — and, at the registry, a dispatch that resolved its id still runs nothing on a set validation rejects (`dispatch_validates_first`). The converse holds too: a settled or pending result, or an `ExecutionFailed`, is reachable only past an accepted validation (`resolver_runs_only_validated`). Validation is characterised EXACTLY rather than soundly: it accepts precisely the sets whose every binding addresses a declared param with a `Null` or an in-type cell and that leave no required name unbound (`validate_params_exact`), the refusal is one of its own three classes (`validate_params_shape`), and a refusal is truthful — an `UnknownParam` names a bound name no param declares and lists the declared ones, a `ParamTypeMismatch` names a declared param, its declared type and a DIFFERENT type the bound cell really has (`refusal_is_truthful`), and a `RequiredParamsUnbound` names only declared names the args really leave out (`unbound_required_truthful`).

THE ENVELOPE HAS NO FOURTH OUTCOME, on this seam as on its sibling. The resolver answers in `Deferred<QueryResult>` (Phase 198), and an invocation past an accepted validation carries its `Ready` or `Pending` and nothing else: a resolver's `Failed m` crossed into the enumerated `ExecutionFailed (m, [])` at the seam, so `Ok (Failed _)` is unreachable rather than merely unproduced, for every resolver and every argument set alike (`invoke_never_ok_failed`), and through the registry, where a host actually reaches the seam (`dispatch_never_ok_failed`). `queryLaws` samples the same claim on the shipped seam over three drawn answers; this is it over all resolvers. The envelope's combinators are outside the model and stay `deferredLaws`'s.

An id is in `QueryRegistry.enumerate`'s output exactly when `QueryRegistry.tryFind` resolves it, and `dispatch` raises `NoSuchQuery` exactly off that enumeration (`no_such_iff_unregistered`) — no hidden entry, no phantom one. A resolved id dispatches to ITS declaration's `invoke` (`registered_dispatches`); `register` refuses a held id (`register_refuses_duplicate`) and extends by exactly one entry otherwise (`register_extends`); and a registry built by `register` from `empty` holds distinct ids (`register_keeps_distinct`), which is what makes a capture key's id prefix name ONE declaration. Membership, not order: production's `Map` sorts the enumeration by id and the model holds the map as a list, so the sorted order is `queryLaws`'s to certify and is outside the theorem.

The Phase 27 capture key reads the declaration through its `Id` ALONE and the arguments through their name-sorted canonical form alone: two declarations sharing an id — whatever else they declare — and two argument lists binding the same DISTINCT names to the same cells in ANY order key identically, under any hash and any int and float renderer, given only that the name comparator is a total order. The order half rests on `sorted_unique`: two name-sorted lists with distinct names holding the same bindings are the same list. The id half needs no premise at all (`invocation_key_id_only`). That the key reads no resolver answer and no clock is NOT a lemma here and is not dressed as one: `invocationKey` is handed neither, so in a pure total function that independence is the function's type. Distinct names are a real hypothesis and not a convenience — `List.sortBy` is stable, so two bindings under ONE name keep the caller's order and the key moves with it.

THE FIRST FINDING. EVERY declaration — whatever it marks `Required` — accepts the argument set that binds each of its params to `Null`. `validateParams`'s step 1 treats a `Null` cell as type-agnostic absence and passes it; step 2 asks only whether the NAME is a key of the argument map, and it is. So `Required` constrains the presence of a name and never of a value, and a resolver is reached with its required param absent. `QueryParam`'s doc comment says a bound cell must agree with the type "(or be `Null` when not required)"; the code accepts it when required as well. Asserted on the shipped seam by the differential's fourth case. Reported, not fixed here: this phase changes no behaviour of `Fuaran.Core.Query`, and the fix shape — step 2 counting a `Null` binding of a required param as unbound — changes what a public function accepts.

THE SECOND FINDING. `invocationKey`'s canonical string joins `name=cellKey` pairs with NO separator, so a string cell can spell the next binding: for one declaration (`a` required, `b` optional, both strings) the two DIFFERENT accepted argument sets `[a = "1b=s2"]` and `[a = "1"; b = "2"]` share the canonical string `a=s1b=s2`, and therefore share a capture key under EVERY hash — the collision is in the pre-image, before `Hash.fnv1a` is consulted.
